parsedVerdict.reasoning: PlaceOrderUseCase.execute does the work an application-layer use case is expected to do. It checks the shape of the incoming request, builds domain objects (OrderItem, Order), calls the domain service and repository abstractions (StockReservationService.reserve, OrderRepository.save), and returns a DTO through toOrderDto. The file has no persistence code: no SQL, ORM or file I/O. It has no transport or framework code either: no HTTP request or response objects, status codes or framework decorators. The checks on customerId, items and productId test the type and presence of raw input, which is boundary validation for untyped request data. One check could be read as business logic: 'items must be non-empty' overlaps with a rule an Order might enforce itself. Even so, it is phrased as a check on the request. The real business rules, such as quantity checks, stock reservation logic and order invariants, are left to the domain (for example, quantity is passed through unchecked to the OrderItem constructor). No ADR prose was given to contradict this.
